data.title: Pennsylvania Democrat says he 'might' challenge Fetterman in 2028
data.description:
Pennsylvania Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said Sunday he “might” mount a primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) in 2028.

“I might, I haven’t decided that. And to be really blunt, I’m doing everything I can right now to help Democrats in Pennsylvania flip congressional seats to give [Pennsylvania Gov.] Josh Shapiro a governing majority in the state Senate and grow the majority in the state House,” Deluzio told host Chris Stirewalt on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

Deluzio later said, “John Fetterman’s nowhere to be seen on the campaign trail. And again, to be very blunt, I don’t think there’s any Democrat in Pennsylvania who wants him campaigning with them, even if he wouldn’t show up.

“So I’m focused on doing what we can do right now to win, and I’ll deal with 2028 when we get past the [midterms].”

Democrats inside and outside of Pennsylvania have taken Fetterman to task throughout the last 18 months, as the first-term senator has sided with President Trump and the GOP on multiple issues — including on the Iran war, with Fetterman voting against every Senate war powers resolution introduced in the upper chamber.

Criticism of Fetterman also ramped up after The Wall Street Journal published a piece on Friday outlining Fetterman’s alleged lack of commitment to his duties as a senator. Fetterman has blasted the report as a “hit piece.”

Deluzio was among those to criticize Fetterman, saying Friday that Fetterman “has no sense of duty” to his constituents.

“He is not up for the high office he was elected to — and we in Pennsylvania will do something about it in 2028,” the second-term representative wrote on social platform X.

Fetterman has also criticized his party’s turn against Israel, defending the Israeli military’s campaign in Gaza. Fetterman said in June his party abandoning the country’s Middle Eastern ally would be a red line. 

“If our party ever becomes — and just makes it official — the anti-Israel party, that’s when I would leave,” he told Alexander Bolton at the Hill Nation Summit.

Roughly half of Democrats believe that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, according to a poll conducted in June by The Associated Press and NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.

Last year, Fetterman voted in line with Trump’s position 28 percent of the time, the most of any Senate Democrat, per data from VoteHub.

data.title: Hinojosa on Trump $10 million Paxton race investment: 'I welcome the attention on Texas'
data.description:
Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa (D) embraced the new spotlight on her state brought on by the unexpectedly close Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton.

“You are running in a state President Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points. He just announced, as I mentioned, that $10 million investment to boost Republican chances in the Texas Senate race. Are you concerned that all of this will, in fact, energize GOP voters in Texas?” CNN’s Dana Bash asked Hinojosa, a representative in the state’s House.

“No, actually not at all. If you look at the polling, President Trump is underwater, Greg Abbott is underwater and people are tired of this politics as usual. People want change in Texas. They’re galvanizing, organizing. We’re building real momentum in this race,” the Democrat replied.

She added, “So, I welcome the attention on Texas. Texas is battleground in 2026. If you don’t believe it, look at what Republicans are doing. But that’s what I hear every day on the campaign trail.”

Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., gave $10 million to Texas attorney general’s Senate campaign, per Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings published over the weekend.

In a poll from late last month, incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) was leading Hinojosa in the race by 7 percentage points, earning 48 percent of respondents’ support. Just 1 percent of those polled backed the Libertarian third-party candidate, while the remaining 8 percent were undecided and 1 percent said they didn’t plan to vote.

Hinojosa showdown in the Lone Star State come as Democrats look to make key gains in the midterms amid rocky political territory for the GOP. Some polls have placed Talarico, another Democratic state representative, ahead of Paxton for Texas’ open Senate seat — which a Republican has occupied for the past three decades.

In recent years, Texas Democrats have sought to notch statewide electoral wins but haven’t had much success, such as the 2018 Senate race between Rep. Beto O’Rourke (D) and incumbent Sen. Ted Cruz (R).

data.title: Carr: FCC 'looking at a lot of actions' after Trump urged 'punishment' for NBC's Welker
data.description:
Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr on Sunday said he is “looking at a lot of actions” to carry out after President Trump urged that the agency punish NBC News’s Kristen Welker.

Carr appeared on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing” with Peter Doocy and said that networks are intended to operate in the public interest and “not some sort of narrow partisan interest.”

“I think President Trump is over the target, and we’re looking at a lot of actions,” he continued. “For instance, there’s a lot of interest right now in fake polls that are out there and so the FCC may put guidance out soon to remind broadcasters about their obligations with respect to not air fake polls, particularly if they’re done to suppress people heading into the fall.”

Welker angered the president last Sunday while teasing an upcoming episode of NBC News’s “Meet the Press” on its Washington, D.C., affiliate earlier in the day. She said Trump is “going to loom large over” the midterm elections while also noting that Trump-endorsed candidates have had “mixed results” during the Republican primaries.

Trump has compiled a 96-percent winning record in this year’s primaries, according to Ballotpedia. Those who have lost include Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, Rep. Randy Feenstra (R-Iowa), MyPillow founder Mike Lindell and South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette.

“How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves?” Trump wrote last week on Truth Social. “Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment.”

NBC News said it stands by Welker, calling her “one of the best in the business.”

Trump has frequently called on the FCC, historically an independent commission, to apply pressure on leading broadcasters throughout his second term. Carr has launched investigations into NBC and ABC’s diversity, equity and inclusion hiring practices.

He and Trump have praised CBS News under its new editor Bar Weiss, previously a columnist, as the network is under parent company Paramount Skydance, led by Trump ally and billionaire David Ellison.

Critics have denounced the president’s use of the FCC as a tool to intimidate journalists ahead of the midterms.

Some Republicans, however, have warned against enforcing regulatory penalties on broadcasters, particularly over ABC’s actions after Jimmy Kimmel was suspended for comments he made after conservative activist Charlie Kirk was killed last September.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), chair of the Senate Commerce Committee, warned last year that Carr’s threats of action against ABC were “dangerous as hell.”

data.title: Washington's affordability debate is missing wages
data.description:
When Angelica Hernandez joined a union, her McDonald’s manager warned her that the company had an army of lawyers, the union would rob her, and she would end up living under a bridge. For three years, Hernandez had resisted joining, afraid of retaliation or losing her job. What finally pushed her to sign on was the intimidation itself.

“If I end up living under a bridge,” she remembered thinking, “I’m going to fight to make sure it doesn’t happen to others.”

Her story contains the missing half of America’s affordability debate. Politicians talk about making rent, groceries, health care, and child care cheaper. They talk much less about whether workers earn enough to keep pace.

With the midterms approaching, affordability has become the defining economic issue of American politics. But it is too often framed as a crisis of prices alone, as though paychecks were fixed and the only solution was to make things cheaper.

Prices and wages come down to the same question: Does a job pay enough to live?

The Fight for $15 forced that question onto the national agenda. When roughly 200 fast-food workers walked off their jobs in New York City in November 2012, they sought more than double the federal minimum wage. The demand was dismissed as unserious. President Obama was calling for a $9 minimum wage; leading Democrats considered $10.10 ambitious. Yet workers chose a number that reflected what survival required rather than what Washington considered plausible.

By the end of 2026, 79 jurisdictions will have reached or exceeded a $15 minimum wage. The National Employment Law Project estimates that the movement helped produce $150 billion in raises for 26 million workers. It also widened the fight to include predictable schedules, paid sick leave, and a voice in setting standards.

The movement taught the country that a winning wage demand cannot remain frozen in time. Adjusted for inflation, the $15 workers demanded in 2012 would be worth about $21.65 today. Yet the federal minimum remains at $7.25, where it has been since 2009, even as roughly 14 million workers still earn less than $15 an hour.

In June 2026, 55 percent of Oklahoma voters rejected a ballot measure that would have raised the state minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 by 2029 and indexed it to the cost of living thereafter.

Opponents argued that the increase would destroy jobs and raise prices. The defeat showed how easily the language of affordability can be turned against higher wages.

The Fight for $15 also fell short of its full promise. It won enormous wage gains without winning widespread collective-bargaining rights for fast-food workers. Workers who became public faces of the campaign did not always gain a permanent role in the institutions making decisions about their lives. I had encountered that dynamic before. During the 2024 presidential campaign, I organized across Arizona, including Native communities that national politicians often visit when electoral margins are close and leave once votes are counted. On a trip to Havasupai, the tribal chairwoman described years of underinvestment. As we prepared to leave, she took my hand and told me something I have not forgotten. “When you are in a room with power, bring us into it.”

I had understood her words as a charge to carry a community’s concerns into powerful rooms.

Listening later to worker leaders from the Fight for $15 describe what happened after the strikes ended and the cameras disappeared, I understood them differently. Being heard by those with power is different from possessing power yourself.

A credible affordability agenda must address both wages and the power workers need to secure them. Congress should set a meaningful national wage floor and index it to inflation or the national median wage. States should retain the ability to set higher standards where living costs demand them. But wage laws alone are not enough. Workers need institutions that give them an enduring voice.

California’s Fast-Food Council, which brings workers, employers, and public officials into the process of setting industry standards, offers one model. Stronger unions, sector-wide bargaining, worker standards boards, and enforceable protections against retaliation offer others.

This is where the affordability agenda has been thinnest. A tax credit can deliver relief. A price cap can reduce a bill. A minimum-wage law can increase a paycheck. Yet, none of those policies gives working people the collective power to shape the next decision, enforce the last one, or prevent their gains from being eroded.

Candidates running on affordability this fall should answer three questions: What wage should a full-time job pay? What mechanism will keep that wage from losing value? And what institutions will give workers the power to defend it after Election Day?

The Fight for $15 supplied the missing logic in today’s affordability debate. Its central insight is that economic security depends on what people earn as well as what they pay. The danger is that politicians will embrace that insight while leaving behind the workers who gave it meaning.

Hernandez learned that asking for more became less frightening once she no longer had to ask alone. A true affordability agenda would carry that lesson forward. A job should pay enough to build a life, and workers should possess enough power to defend what they build.

Dylan Baca is a researcher, writer and former political organizer who has led youth and Native voter engagement efforts in Arizona and nationally. Baca is a graduate of Columbia University, where he studied political science and American studies.

data.title: Lawler disagrees with Trump on Iran war: 'It is certainly not small potatoes'
data.description:
Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) on Sunday broke with President Trump regarding the commander in chief’s recent statement about the Iran war where he downplayed the conflict.

“Any time you are at war or in a military escalation, it is certainly not small potatoes. It is serious. I think we all recognize that,” Lawler told CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union,” referencing recent comments from the president.

“Ensuring Iran does not possess a nuclear weapon, stopping them from continuing to finance terrorism, Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, and other terror proxies, stopping them from mass-producing ballistic missiles, drones, which are being used by Russia against Ukraine, is critical,” he added.

In the Oval Office on Friday, Trump said he was referring to the Iran war as “a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us.”

“It’s not a big thing,” the president added.

The Iran war just passed the six-month mark, with the fighting straining U.S. relationships with historic allies, driving up oil and gas prices and proving unpopular with the American public in recent polling.

On Sunday, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said he did not “want to have an opinion” on the direction of gas prices Americans are paying, which are above $4 per gallon on average.

“You said on this show five months ago that high gas prices had peaked, but between not just the Iran war, but the Russia-Ukraine war and the U.S.’s own dwindling reserves, isn’t it possible gas prices could go up even more?” Bash asked Wright on “State of the Union.”

“Look, I don’t want to have an opinion on that, but if you look at the futures market right now, what can you buy gasoline for two months in advance from where we are today? It’s down more than 30 cents a gallon from where it is today,” Wright responded.

data.title: Why the golf industry largely supports permanent daylight saving time
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – In less than two months, every clock in the U.S. will be on standard time, with the end of daylight saving time coming as early as possible this year.

That could change if the Senate acts quickly on a bill that would make daylight saving time permanent in the U.S. The country has observed year-round daylight saving time for stretches before, but it never lasted long.

There are many who do not support “locking the clocks,” pointing to the drawbacks it may have for our health, the impacts it would have on how they practice religion, and the safety concerns associated with when the sun would rise, especially in winter.

There are, however, proponents of making daylight saving time permanent, including President Trump. An industry long associated with Trump largely agrees.

Golfers are among those who have come out in support of daylight saving time, both in its current format and in the hopes of permanent observance. Course owners and industry advocates told The Associated Press last year that, if the U.S. were to observe permanent standard time, it could lead to a loss in business.

There isn’t unanimous agreement on what should happen to the clocks among members of the National Golf Course Owners Association (NGCOA), CEO Jay Karen told Nexstar via email. Karen testified before a Senate committee and a House subcommittee last year regarding daylight saving time legislation.

About two-thirds of NGCOA’s members support permanent daylight saving time, Karen explained, while a quarter are content with the current twice-a-year changing of the clocks.

“So, if Congress and the White House intend to change the law and stop changing the clocks, they must choose either permanent Daylight Saving Time or permanent Standard Time,” he said. “If they must choose, we support permanent DST.”

Under permanent daylight saving time, it’s winters that would feel vastly different than they do now. In much of the U.S., the sun wouldn’t rise until after 8 a.m. for at least part of the winter. For some, the sun wouldn’t come up until after 9 a.m. The trade-off, though, would be later sunsets in winter.

That extra daylight in the afternoons could allow golf courses the opportunity to “eke out more activity,” Karen explained. He acknowledged, though, that any golf courses that close for the winter, like those in the northern U.S., would not be impacted by “any change in the law.”

If standard time were to become permanent, summer sunsets would happen an hour earlier than they do now. For much of the summer, that could mean sunsets prior to 7 p.m. Industry experts in Nebraska and Utah came out strongly against local attempts to make standard time permanent, saying the move could lead to lost revenue for golf courses in their respective states. Karen told the AP that year-round standard time would harm “thousands of courses.”

There is another daylight saving time-related bill that could still find its way through Congress. The Daylight Act of 2026 would make “half” daylight saving time permanent. Instead of clocks falling back an hour in November, for example, they would fall back 30 minutes.

When asked about this approach to locking the clocks, Karen said that “any bill that allows for more recreational daylight, meaning when sunshine aligns with people’s availability to get outside and exercise, is favorable for our industry.”

“I’d like to point out that this is about much more than golf,” he added. “Having extra time to enjoy healthy outdoor activities that require sunlight is good for physical and mental health, as well as our economy. It’s a win-win.”

You may be running out of afternoon tee times right now. Through September, parts of the country will lose an hour or more of daylight.

Unless the Senate takes up and passes the Sunshine Protection Act soon, you can expect your clocks to fall back an hour on Nov. 1.

data.title: The hidden cost of losing your community bank: disruptive innovation
data.description:
In July, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law, carrying a provision that drew almost no attention. It directs federal banking regulators to run a two-year pilot that makes it easier to charter new community banks — with particular attention to rural areas — and gives banks chartered between 2026 and 2028 a phase-in period to meet capital requirements. Congress has decided the country needs more small banks.

Bank regulators are moving the other way. Bank mergers hit a four-year high in 2025, and both the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. have rolled back merger review rules that slowed the process. Washington is now trying to seed community banks with one hand while clearing the path to absorb them with the other.

Whether that tradeoff is worth making depends on a question that the banking consolidation debate has mostly skipped. The debate has focused almost entirely on competition and consumer prices. It has largely ignored something harder to measure and easier to lose: innovation.

Our recent research examined the relationship between banking consolidation and innovation across all 50 states from 1994 to 2020. We found that the issue is not simply whether a banking market is concentrated. What matters is whether a handful of very large banks dominate it.

In those markets, something specific happens: the kind of innovation that gets funded changes. Regions where mega-banks hold large market shares produce more incremental patents that improve existing products and fewer disruptive ones that create entirely new industries.

The distinction matters. Disruptive innovation is what produces the next breakthrough technology, the next category-defining company. It is also the hardest to finance. Studies of patents and scientific papers show that truly disruptive ideas have declined sharply across many sectors in recent decades. Our findings suggest that the structure of the banking system is one reason.

Typically, large banks standardize lending criteria such as credit scores, collateral and cash flow. These may work in your typical businesses with established reputation and assets, but a young company might struggle to pass an algorithm-driven loan review, no matter how promising.

Community banks operate differently from their counterparts. While they also care about traditional lending metrics, they fill a gap in their market by using their local knowledge to evaluate borrowers that large banks typically ignore. Someone who knows the community can make decisions based on local context, not just credit scores. This type of lending is a crucial source of funding that has historically backed startups driving major innovations. But recently, there has been a shift in the lending market.

That financing channel is shrinking fast. The number of banking institutions in the United States decreased from approximately 13,000 in 1994 to about 7,000 by 2020. Currently, there are only 4,336 FDIC-insured institutions remaining, representing a 35 percent decline since 2005. Since the financial crisis, fewer than 90 new banks have been established nationwide. As a result, over 12 million Americans now live in banking deserts, which are communities that lack any physical bank branches.

Venture capital has not filled the gap. It is highly concentrated geographically and focused on a narrow set of industries. Rural communities across the Great Plains, Appalachia and the Deep South receive less than 1 percent of all venture capital funding. The sectors that sustain rural and small-town economies, agriculture, manufacturing, energy and local services, are largely invisible to venture investors.

Banking consolidation isn’t always a bad thing. Our research shows that when concentration levels are moderate, it can actually spur innovation. The problem is when a handful of large institutions dominate the market. In those markets, lending tends to favor safer, more conventional investments.

If policymakers are serious about sustaining American innovation, they should consider what happens downstream of bank mergers. The cost of losing a community bank is not just one fewer name on a Main Street sign. It is one fewer institution willing to take a chance on the ideas that could define the next generation of the American economy.

Oudom Hean is an associate professor and Sean Schiefelbein is his research assistant at North Dakota State University. They are co-authors of the new working paper “Banking Consolidation and Innovation in the United States.”

data.title: Wright says Iran war worth it to 'reset' Middle East
data.description:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday the Iran war is necessary, arguing the U.S. needs to “reset” the Middle East.

During an interview on ABC’s “This Week,” Wright reiterated the longstanding talking point from administration officials that the goal of the conflict is to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

“A nuclear armed Iran is an existential threat, not just for the region, but for the world economy,” he told host Martha Raddatz.

“I’m very proud of President Trump, not just kicking this can down the road like previous presidents have done, but saying we’ve got to end that capability,” Wright added. “We’ve got to reset the Middle East so it can have generations of peace and prosperity.”

The war, in its seventh month, has resulted in the deaths of 18 American service members and thousands of Iranian civilians. The U.S. and Iran continued to exchange strikes this weekend, and there is no sign of a deal to permanently end hostilities.

The conflict has also come with economic costs for the U.S., stemming from the Iranian military’s restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. 

The national average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly $4.14 on Sunday, more than six months after it was below $3 just days before the U.S. and Israel launched the war, according to AAA.

Labor Day weekend travelers, in fact, are seeing the highest prices at the pump on record, AAA reported on Thursday.

Wright said Sunday that daily transit in the Strait of Hormuz is at roughly “two-thirds” of where it stood before the war, as the U.S. military has sought to escort tankers through the waterway. 

The Energy secretary noted his estimate of transit in the strait includes oil passing through pipelines.

“They’re clinging on to power as the United States continues to escalate the volume of oil that transits through the Strait of Hormuz,” Wright said, referring to the Islamic Republic regime.

data.title: Trump administration makes new appeal for Supreme Court to allow mail voting changes ahead of midterms
data.description:
The Trump administration on Sunday again asked the Supreme Court to allow it to restrict mail-in voting this election cycle.

In a 40-page emergency application, Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the justices to immediately permit the administration to bar the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) from sending mail-in ballots to residents of states that have not submitted a list of eligible voters based on citizenship data.

Sauer argued the administration is likely to succeed on the merits in two cases concerning the policy — one a group of Democratic-led states brought against the USPS and another the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts brought against the administration.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani on Friday indefinitely halted the USPS plan while lower courts decided on the policy. Her ruling came on the day North Carolina began to mail ballots to residents, which Sauer noted in his Sunday filing.

Talwani, an appointee of former President Obama, halted the administration from carrying out the plan a day after Sauer submitted an initial stay application to the Supreme Court. But in filing the administration’s new request for a stay of Talwani’s preliminary injunction, the solicitor general withdrew his Thursday filing.

The Supreme Court, which is on recess, will decide the case in an expedited fashion. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, one of the three liberals on the high court, will rule on the administration’s new request.

In his Sunday filing, Sauer wrote the policy “is a valid exercise” of the USPS’s authority, and “does not regulate state administration” of elections.

“The Rule ensures that States remain responsible for determining voter eligibility and eligibility to vote by mail, and it does not dictate ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures,” he wrote.

“The Rule thus plainly does not seize control of States’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail,” Sauer added. 

But Sophia Lin Lakin, the director of the American Civil Liberties Union’s Voting Rights Projects, blasted the USPS policy as “unconstitutional” and accused the Trump administration of “running” to the Supreme Court to circumvent lower court rulings earlier this week. 

“The only emergency here is the one the administration created,” added Lakin, whose organization is representing some of the challengers to the administration’s rule. “The court’s temporary order preserves the voting procedures Americans have relied on for years, and it should stand.”

data.title: White House faces mifepristone test
data.description:
The Trump administration is set to face another key test on abortion, with two months to go until the midterm elections.

A three-judge panel on the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans is poised to hear oral arguments next week in a case that could eventually restrict the nationwide distribution of the abortion drug mifepristone.   

Medication has become the most common method of abortion since Roe v. Wade was overturned in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, with much of that increase coming from telehealth prescriptions.

The Biden administration loosened telehealth regulations in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, allowing a surge of pills to be prescribed through telehealth, in pharmacies and through the mail.   

Louisiana, which has almost completely banned abortion, objected to the policy and sued.  

The state argued that the FDA’s permissive rules undercut its near-total abortion ban and were a violation of the state’s sovereignty. Louisiana also asserted the FDA didn’t have enough safety data to roll back the in-person dispensing requirement. 

According to the Guttmacher Institute, a think tank that supports abortion access, about 91,000 abortions were provided last year via telehealth prescription of abortion medication sent by mail to states with bans, including more than 9,300 in Louisiana. 

“The stakes in this case are enormous,” Kelly Baden, Vice President for U.S. Policy & Communications at Guttmacher said in a statement. “Patients, providers, and communities have endured nonstop attacks on abortion access— the Fifth Circuit must reject this baseless case and affirm the status quo for nationwide access to medication abortion.” 

The Louisiana case has put the Trump administration in an awkward political bind: it won’t defend moves made by the Biden administration, but Attorney General Todd Blanche has not yet settled the lawsuit, much to the disappointment of conservatives who have been pressuring him.     

“The Trump administration could resolve this issue tomorrow by settling our case. Absolutely,” said Gabriella McIntyre, legal counsel of Alliance Defending Freedom, which is helping to argue the case for Louisiana and one of its residents, a co-plaintiff who says her then-boyfriend coerced her into taking abortion pills. 

During his confirmation hearing, Blanche pledged to take action to stop mifepristone from being available through the mail.   

“You know, I’ve seen video myself of what appears to be pills coming even from overseas to young women, and doesn’t matter who applies for it, anybody can get it. There’s no instructions; they just come dumped out of a little plastic bag, and it’s wrong,” Blanche said. “And I very much commit our resources to stopping this.”  

During a private call with faith leaders, Blanche hinted that restrictions on mail-order abortion drugs are coming.  

The administration is “putting practices and policies in place so that other states and other organizations” can’t send abortion pills through the mail to states where they are banned, he said. 

But meanwhile, the Justice Department has been urging courts to put mifepristone lawsuits on hold until FDA finishes a safety review. 

An administration official said in June the retrospective analysis of data is likely to take six months to complete, but initial results could be released earlier. The district court judge in Louisiana set an Oct. 7 deadline for a status update, meaning some of the FDA’s efforts will be clear just weeks before the election.  

Anti-abortion groups hope the review will result in restrictions on mifepristone, but they want the FDA to move faster. The administration says the work takes time, but conservative states aren’t waiting. 

The Louisiana case is one of three federal lawsuits that could affect telehealth access to mifepristone nationwide. The others are being considered in Missouri and Texas. 

The Texas case was paused by a federal judge on Aug. 31, while the Missouri case is still being briefed.  

In Louisiana, a federal district judge said the state had a strong case but decided to pause the lawsuit while FDA’s review was in progress. Louisiana appealed, and the 5th Circuit in May ruled in favor of the state, temporarily blocking telehealth prescriptions of mifepristone nationwide.  

The Supreme Court then paused the 5th Circuit’s ruling and sent the case back, after two manufacturers of mifepristone appealed. Notably, the Justice Department declined to weigh in, though other GOP states and members of Congress did.   

McIntyre said the Trump administration’s silence on the merits of the case speaks volumes, because it means the administration doesn’t believe the FDA’s actions were defensible.  

She expects much of Wednesday’s arguments to focus on whether Louisiana has standing to argue for a nationwide ruling. 

“If Louisiana wins, we’re going to see for the first time truly what it looks like for pro-life states to actually be able to enforce their pro-life laws protecting the unborn. That was the promise of Dobbs,” McIntyre said. 

Katie Keith, director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown University’s O’Neill Institute, agreed that the administration’s attempt to thread a political needle may backfire. 

“They’re not being able to have it both ways on this,” Keith said. “By trying to sort of stay out of it and just say we’re doing our review, that position has actively been used against them in court [and] could be the thing that the courts point to … to actually limit access to the drug.” 

The FDA has repeatedly found mifepristone is safe and that a medication abortion regimen that includes mifepristone and a second drug, misoprostol, is a safe and effective alternative to surgical abortions.     

Mifepristone has been used by more than 7.5 million people in the U.S. for medication abortion and miscarriage care since the FDA approved it more than two decades ago.  A series of agency actions in 2016 and 2023 loosened access to the drug, and abortion opponents have been strategizing attacks ever since. 

The first major assault began in 2022, when anti-abortion doctors and medical organizations sued to try to revoke the original approval of mifepristone.  

While lower courts agreed, the Supreme Court in 2024 unanimously upheld access to mifepristone on a technicality, ruling that doctors and medical groups opposed to abortion did not have a legal right to sue. 

The 5th Circuit is considered to be of the most conservative appeals courts in the country, but Wednesday’s panel includes two judges appointed by Democratic presidents; one from former President Obama, and one from former President Biden. 

Greer Donley, an abortion law expert and professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Law, said no matter what the appeals court eventually rules, the case is almost certainly going to the Supreme Court.  

Given the FDA’s ongoing review, the other mifepristone cases around the country, and the likelihood of the high court’s involvement, “it makes me feel like this is just all political theater,” Donley said.
